title: Zoho's Sridhar Vembu Flags the Uncomfortable Truth: AI Is Writing More Code, but Software Isn't Getting Better
excerpt: The developer productivity paradox — more output, same problems — and why it matters for India's five-million-strong tech workforce
body:
Sridhar Vembu has a reputation for saying unfashionable things at exactly the right moment. The Zoho founder, who famously relocated from Silicon Valley to a Tamil Nadu village, has now turned his contrarian gaze on the tech industry's most sacred assumption: that artificial intelligence is making software development dramatically more productive.

## The Paradox

In a series of public remarks and posts this month, Vembu laid out what he calls the "developer productivity paradox." The argument is deceptively simple. AI coding assistants — tools like GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and a growing ecosystem of code-generation models — have unquestionably increased the volume of code being written. Developers report generating code 30 to 50 per cent faster. But Vembu contends that this surge in output has not translated into a proportional improvement in software quality, maintainability, or overall engineering productivity.

"There is virtually no real understanding in AI-generated code," Vembu wrote, pointing to the growing problem of what the industry calls "AI technical debt" — code that works on first pass but is poorly structured, hard to debug, and expensive to maintain over time.

## Context and Background

Vembu's warning arrives at a moment of reckoning. The global software industry has spent the past two years in a frenzy of AI adoption, with companies racing to integrate generative AI into every stage of the development pipeline. The promise was transformative: fewer engineers doing more work, faster product cycles, lower costs.

The reality is messier. Multiple studies in 2025 and early 2026 have shown that while AI tools accelerate certain narrow tasks — boilerplate code, documentation, simple function generation — they struggle with complex system architecture, edge-case handling, and the kind of contextual judgement that experienced engineers bring. A widely cited Stack Overflow developer survey found that while 78 per cent of developers now use AI tools, only 34 per cent reported meaningful productivity gains in end-to-end project delivery.

Meanwhile, the costs of AI implementation have proven far higher than anticipated. Enterprise licences for AI coding tools, the compute required to run them, and the engineering time spent reviewing and fixing AI-generated output have created a new expense line that, for many companies, rivals the headcount savings they were meant to deliver.

## Current Developments

Vembu's remarks come as Zoho itself is charting a distinctive path. The company, which has over 100 million users globally and builds its entire product suite in-house, has been developing AI capabilities internally rather than relying on third-party models. Zoho recently announced a 99 enterprise hardware device — featuring a Qualcomm Snapdragon processor, 16 GB of RAM, and 512 GB of storage — designed to run AI workloads locally, keeping data on-premises.

The move is vintage Vembu: build it yourself, keep it private, price it for the real market rather than the venture-capital-inflated one. It also reflects his broader thesis that the current AI gold rush, dominated by a handful of American hyperscalers, poses structural risks to India's technology ecosystem.

Vembu has been particularly vocal about what he sees as an accelerating brain drain. India's best computer science graduates, he argues, are being hoovered up by global AI labs, leaving the domestic tech sector — which employs over five million people — with a thinning talent pool at the precise moment it needs deep expertise to navigate the AI transition.

## Diaspora Impact

For the hundreds of thousands of Indian-origin software engineers working in Silicon Valley, Seattle, Bangalore, and beyond, Vembu's paradox is not academic. It cuts to the heart of career anxieties that have intensified since the layoff waves of 2023-24. If AI is not actually replacing developers but is instead reshuffling the value chain — making code generation cheap while making system thinking premium — then the skills that matter are shifting faster than most engineers' resumes can keep up.

The diaspora's tech workforce is disproportionately represented in the middle tiers of software engineering — the roles most exposed to AI disruption. Vembu's implicit argument is that India, and Indians abroad, should be investing not in learning to use AI tools but in developing the deeper engineering judgement that AI cannot replicate.

## What is Next

The developer productivity paradox is unlikely to be resolved by better models alone. As Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei warned in separate remarks this month, AI's trajectory could lead to "software company collapse" if firms mistake faster code generation for faster value creation. The Gates Foundation and Anthropic have also announced a 00 million partnership to deploy AI in global health and education — an acknowledgement that AI's most productive applications may lie outside the software factory floor.

Vembu, characteristically, is betting on a different future — one where smaller, private, Indian-built AI tools serve the real economy rather than the hype cycle. Whether that bet pays off will depend on whether the industry listens to the paradox before it proves the point the hard way.
